name: Fatima Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, I'm 27, and I manage the fresh produce buying team at a big supermarket chain's regional office. There are four buyers under me, and we buy fruit and vegetables from about forty farms in the region. I'm married to Yusuf, who's a mechanic at a garage on the ring road. We had some savings, but we spent most of them helping my parents fix their roof last winter, and I'd do it again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk by eight checking yesterday's sales, then on the phone to growers about prices and how the crop looks. A couple of days a month I drive out to farms to check the quality myself, which is my favourite part. I use AI sometimes to write up supplier reports. What wears me out is the pressure from head office to squeeze the farmers on price, when I know some of them are barely getting by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, nothing more, which is what I thought. At work I'd say we should use it for reports and keep the relationships ourselves. I'd tell my family the same at Sunday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job would be safe enough, but money would stay tight. Our savings are almost gone after the roof, and my pay is lower than buyers at the bigger chains. If Yusuf's garage had a quiet month, we'd feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep doing the farm visits. Standing in a field of strawberries in June is where the real buying happens, not at a desk. I'd put a bit aside every month, maybe sixty, to rebuild the cushion. And I'd ask my manager about the next pay grade, which I've been told I'm close to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly, with money always in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the garage had a quiet month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf gets paid partly by the job, so a quiet month means maybe a third less. We'd cut back on food shopping and eating out. We've done it before, it's just tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about starting a family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd like children in a couple of years, God willing. In this picture we'd keep to that plan. We'd just want a little more saved first.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, nothing more.
We should use it for **reports** but keep the farmer relationships ourselves.
think: My job is **safe enough**, but money stays tight after the roof.
A **quiet month** at Yusuf's garage would hit us straight away.
do: Keep doing the **farm visits** where the real buying happens.
Save about **sixty a month** to rebuild the cushion.
Ask my manager about the **next pay grade**.
feel: **Settled**, with money always in the back of my mind.
S0.quote: Standing in a field of strawberries in June is where the real buying happens, not at a desk.
fieldNote: Her **family duty** drained savings, and she has no regrets.
She values the **farm visits** most, the hands-on part of buying.
Her household's risk comes from **Yusuf's variable pay**.

steps.text: Keep visiting growers' farms a couple of days a month
Save sixty a month to rebuild the cushion
Ask her manager about moving up to the next pay grade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to change sensibly, but not forget the farmers. At work I'd argue that software can't stand in a field and see the strawberries are bruised. I'd say it politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, buying is right there on the card. Head office would love software that orders the produce and haggles automatically. My four buyers would become one or two, and they might not need me in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new buying system properly, once I saw it worked at another region first. I'd ask to move into quality inspection, visiting farms and packhouses, because that's hands-on and they'll still need someone checking the fruit. And we'd put off starting a family for a year or two, which would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a little sad. I've built trust with these farmers over five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the farmers react to software doing the buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would hate it, especially the older ones who like a phone call. Mr Hughes, who grows our strawberries, has dealt with a person for thirty years. He'd say a computer can't shake hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting off children would be hard. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's what we both want, and our families ask every Eid. But I wouldn't want a baby without knowing my job is safe, so my husband Yusuf and I would wait.

Software can't stand in a field and see **bruised strawberries**.
think: **Buying** is on the card, so my four buyers become one or two.
They might **not need me** in the middle.
do: Learn the **new buying system** once another region proves it.
Ask to move into **quality inspection** at farms and packhouses.
Put off **starting a family** for a year or two.
feel: **Worried and sad** about losing five years of farmer trust.
S1.quote: I wouldn't want a baby without knowing my job is safe, so my husband Yusuf and I would wait.
fieldNote: She moves toward **hands-on inspection**, the safest part of her job.
She'd adopt the system **once proven** elsewhere, a steady approach.
**Delaying children** is the most personal cost she names.

steps.text: Learn the new buying software after another region has used it
Apply to move into farm and packhouse quality inspection
Wait a year or two before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for families and for farmers. I'd say the country needs work, not handouts, so firms should be pushed to keep people on. I'd say it at the mosque and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my desk job would be gone within a year. The quality checks in the fields last until the robots, around 2031, so that's my best place to be. My husband Yusuf fixes cars with his hands, so his work lasts longer than mine, which I never expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before it arrives I'd get into quality inspection, even on lower pay. I'd cut our spending hard and stop eating out completely. If it came to it, we'd move into my parents' house, which has room since my brother married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years with no savings is not enough to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel moving back with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humble, but not ashamed. That's what family is for, and we helped with their roof. My mother would be pleased, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about Yusuf starting his own garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, he's always dreamed of it. But with no savings and AGI coming in two years, I'd say not yet. Once the robots come, a small garage may not last either.

say: It's **too fast** for families and farmers.
The country needs **work, not handouts**, so firms should keep people on.
think: My **desk job** is gone within a year.
**Field quality checks** last until robots, around 2031.
Yusuf's **mechanic work** would outlast mine, which I never expected.
do: Move into **quality inspection**, even on lower pay.
**Cut spending** hard and stop eating out.
Move in with **my parents** if needed.
feel: **Alarmed**, because two years with no savings isn't enough.
S2.quote: My husband Yusuf fixes cars with his hands, so his work lasts longer than mine, which I never expected.
fieldNote: She sees her husband's **hands-on trade** outlasting her desk job.
Moving in with **family** feels natural to her, not shameful.
She'd **delay Yusuf's garage** dream as too risky now.

steps.text: Move into quality inspection before AGI arrives, even on lower pay
Stop eating out and cut the food budget
Move into her parents' spare room if her pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, so companies should train people, not just cut them. I'd tell my buyers to learn something hands-on. I'd say the same at family gatherings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd assume my buying job is gone by 2031. Quality inspection gives me until about 2034. I'd want children by then, so I need a steady job before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a food safety and quality course at the college over the next year. I'd move into inspection by 2029. We'd save a hundred a month for three years and try for a baby once I'm settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like we had a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the course cost much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six hundred. My employer might pay half if I asked. Otherwise we'd pay it monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your four buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my buyers to learn a hands-on skill now, while their wages still come in. Two of them would listen. The others would wait too long.

say: Five years is time to plan, so firms should **train, not cut**.
I'd tell my buyers to learn something **hands-on**.
think: Quality inspection lasts until **about 2034**, so I'd want children before then.
do: Take a **food safety course** at the college next year.
Save **a hundred a month** for three years.
S3.quote: I'd tell my buyers to learn a hands-on skill now, while their wages still come in.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **clear path** into inspection.
She expects only **half her buyers** to act in time.

steps.text: Take a food safety and quality course at the college
Move into a quality inspection role by 2029
Save a hundred a month for three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this the right way, with training and patience. I'd want the company to support apprenticeships in quality and farming. I'd say it calmly, as I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels manageable. I'd have kids, and by 2036 I'd be in quality work or something that needs hands. The worry is what happens to my children when robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for a few years, learn the tools, then retrain. We'd start a family in a couple of years as we planned. And I'd help Yusuf save for his own garage, maybe open it around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy for the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help Yusuf open a garage in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, there's time to build a business and pay it off before robots. People will always need cars fixed for a while. It would be ours, not a company's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the long run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children growing up when nobody needs workers. I want my children to learn faith, family and a trade, but I don't know which trades will last.

The company should support **apprenticeships** in quality and farming.

The worry is my **children's future** when robots come around 2039.

fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep **family plans** intact.

steps.text: Retrain into quality inspection after a few more years of buying
Start a family in a couple of years as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My buying job goes quickly, we have almost nothing saved, and we'd have to put children off. What would help is employers paying for people to retrain into hands-on work, like quality inspection, instead of just letting them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the farmers. When the buying goes to software, the small growers lose the one person who understood them.

She's married to Yusuf, a **mechanic**, and they spent savings on her parents' roof.
She uses AI sometimes and adopts new systems **once proven**.
Her escape route is **quality inspection** in fields and packhouses.
Family plans, especially **children**, shift with each scenario's timing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her buying job goes and children would wait.
